# Install and run your first capture

Use the [README installation](../README.md#install-from-source) with OCaml
5.5.2, opam and tmux on Linux. The native clients compile a small Linux C helper
and require a C compiler and system headers. This source checkout installs the
libraries; no registry release is available yet.

Activate the local switch in the current shell as shown in the README before
changing to a separate project. This exports the switch choice for `opam exec`
without changing shell startup files or the global default switch.

## Link an installed library

For a blocking program, use a Dune executable with `libtmux` and `libtmux-unix`:

```dune
(executable
 (name main)
 (libraries libtmux libtmux-unix))
```

For the Eio examples, link the Eio backend and the application's runtime entry
point instead:

```dune
(executable
 (name main)
 (libraries libtmux libtmux-eio eio_main))
```

Create `dune-project` with `(lang dune 3.24)`, save the
[graph program](../examples/native_graph.ml) as `main.ml`, and build from that
project. The installed-example check does this outside the repository with a
separate install prefix; it does not depend on source-tree library resolution.

```console
$ opam exec -- dune build
```

## Select an endpoint explicitly

`Endpoint.socket_path` accepts an absolute socket path; `Endpoint.named_socket`
describes tmux's `-L` name. Constructing either performs no I/O. Ordinary
`Client.connect` attaches to an existing daemon and does not start one.

The [private demo setup](../README.md#read-a-real-tmux-graph) creates an owned
socket and a `cat` pane. Run the graph program with the tmux binary and socket
path, or copy its complete source into your project. It captures the graph,
closes its connection and prints retained observations.

A connection identifies the daemon PID twice around pidfd acquisition. The
client and daemon must share a PID namespace and local scratch filesystem;
an accessible socket by itself does not establish those conditions. A stale
source is an error, never permission to reconnect a mutation automatically.

## Run a concurrent application

The [complete Eio example](../examples/native_watch.ml) calls `Eio_main.run`
and `Eio.Switch.run`, then supplies `process_mgr` and `mono_clock` from the
application environment. Use that outer shape in your application. Capturing
and querying values does not require adopting Eio in the pure core.

Expected failures return `result` and print with `Error.pp`. Backend
cancellation propagates separately. Clients and subscriptions belong to their
connecting domain; immutable observations can be shared. Close owned resources
with `Fun.protect` or the supplied Eio switch.

# Start a private tmux server from OCaml

Use `Workspace.submit_bootstrap` when the endpoint is known to be missing.
It creates the first session and binds a client through the same control
connection. The native workspace builder needs no JSON package;
`Workspace.await` performs startup.

For an existing daemon, use `Client.connect`, capture its graph, and create a
session through that client. See [control and recovery](control.md).

## Run the complete program

Complete the [source installation](getting-started.md), then run from the
checkout:

```console
$ opam exec -- dune exec examples/showcase_bootstrap.exe -- tmux
```

The program prints its temporary socket path followed by
`bootstrapped: 1 session, 1 window, 1 pane`. It creates a `bootstrap-demo` session
whose `editor` window runs `/bin/cat -u`, captures the graph, and reads that
snapshot after closing its client.

The [complete source](../examples/showcase_bootstrap.ml) includes its private
directory, tmux configuration, local version discovery and cleanup. To use the
whole program outside this checkout, save it as `main.ml` in the Dune project
from [first use](getting-started.md#link-an-installed-library) with:

```dune
(executable
 (name main)
 (libraries libtmux libtmux-workspace libtmux-unix unix))
```

CI compiles that complete file against installed packages and checks its exact
outcome line, graph assertions, directory cleanup and owned process exit on
tmux 3.3a and 3.8. The [executed inventory](../examples/showcase.json) records
its command and workflow.

## Build, plan, await and capture

The central function receives the binary's discovered version and a new private
socket path. `Config.make`, `Plan.make` and submission perform no I/O; the
function returns a retained execution handle:

<!-- example: examples/showcase_bootstrap.ml#bootstrap -->

```ocaml
let bootstrap ~binary ~version ~directory endpoint =
  let spawn = Spawn.make (Exec { program = "/bin/cat"; args = [ "-u" ] }) in
  let config =
    Config.make ~directory ~session:"bootstrap-demo"
      [ Config.window ~name:"editor" [ Config.pane ~spawn () ] ]
    |> checked Config.pp_error
  in
  let plan =
    Plan.make ~endpoint ~version ~observed:None config |> checked Plan.pp_error
  in
  get (Workspace.submit_bootstrap ~binary plan)
```

Passing [`None`](https://ocaml.org/manual/5.5/api/Option.html#TYPEELTt.None) as the
`observed` argument means the endpoint is known to be missing. The full program
uses a newly created private directory to establish that precondition. A failed
capture must remain an error; treating it as a missing observation discards that
failure and produces the wrong plan. A plan remains advisory; another process
can still change the endpoint before execution.

Keep that handle outside the cleanup scope. Await it, check the receipt, then
borrow its client for the capture:

<!-- example: examples/showcase_bootstrap.ml#await-bootstrap -->

```ocaml
let snapshot =
  protect
    ~finally:(fun () -> get (Workspace.close execution))
    (fun () ->
      let receipt = get (Workspace.await execution) in
      require_success receipt;
      let client = Option.get (Workspace.client execution) in
      get (Client.capture client))
```

`require_success` reports failed steps and compensation before raising. The
[`protect` helper](../examples/showcase_bootstrap.ml#L14) keeps that primary
exception if closing also fails, reporting the cleanup failure separately.
Both helpers are in the complete source.
`Workspace.inspect execution` reads the retained journal after closure; inspect
reported creations and uncertainty before choosing another action. The
program stops without retrying. The
[workspace guide](workspaces.md#collisions-and-recovery) explains those receipts.

`Workspace.client` borrows the bootstrapped client. Close the workspace handle
after using that client; its snapshot stays readable.

## Choose the daemon's lifetime

Bootstrapping owns the new client, not the tmux daemon. Closing the handle
releases that client. The example explicitly configures its private daemon
with `exit-unattached on`, supplied through a small shell exec wrapper. The
daemon and its demonstration pane exit after
the final client detaches. It then removes only its own temporary files.

For an application that keeps the server, choose its normal tmux lifetime
policy and retain the workspace handle while using the borrowed client. An
existing or newly visible daemon does not become owned merely because this
application connected to it. Cancellation and a partial bootstrap can leave
effects; use [retained operation recovery](recovery.md) and the workspace
receipt rather than assuming closure undoes them.

# Sessions, window links and panes

A snapshot contains sessions, global windows, session-specific window links,
panes and captured clients. Entity values are abstract immutable observations.
They remain readable after their client closes.

```text
Session ── Window_link ── Window ── Pane
                index       │
                   another link can share this window
```

A window can be linked to multiple sessions, or linked more than once within
one session. `Session.window_links` retains each context and index.
`Session.windows` returns distinct global windows in first-link order.
`Window.panes` contains that global window's captured panes. Local traversal
performs no I/O, lazy refresh or per-object subprocess calls. Captured client
rows and attached-client counts include the library's control connection when
it is present.

The [graph program](../examples/native_graph.ml) deliberately walks links. To
see the same window in two sessions, run the [README setup](../README.md#read-a-real-tmux-graph),
then create another session:

```console
$ env -u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE tmux \
    -S "$LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR/server" \
    new-session \
    -d \
    -s linked \
    -- "exec cat"
```

Link the demo's window at index 7 in the other session:

```console
$ env -u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE tmux \
    -S "$LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR/server" \
    link-window \
    -d \
    -s @0 \
    -t linked:7
```

```console
$ opam exec -- dune exec examples/native_graph.exe -- \
    tmux "$LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR/server"
```

The same window ID and pane ID appear under both sessions, at their respective
link indexes. The installed-example check asserts both appearances. Remove
only the additional session when finished:

```console
$ env -u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE tmux \
    -S "$LIBTMUX_DEMO_DIR/server" \
    kill-session -t '=linked'
```

An entity ID is scoped to a connection source. `same_entity` requires the same
bound source generation as well as the same entity ID; separate connections
compare unequal even when they observe the same daemon. `same_observation`
also distinguishes captures. Use those operations or explicit `Id.equal`,
rather than polymorphic equality over observations. A valid target does not
make captured names, geometry or membership current.
A link context is an observed session/index/window tuple, not a stable link
incarnation across unlinking or reindexing.

Capture provenance records an acquisition interval. Several tmux commands do
not form an atomic server transaction. Disappearing or conflicting objects
produce a capture error rather than a fabricated empty relationship.

Each entity retains the complete snapshot graph so its relationships remain
available. Retaining one pane from every refresh therefore retains every one
of those captures. Keep scalar summaries when navigation is unnecessary.
`Pane.target` omits the graph but remains bound to its original connection
generation; it is not a durable target for a future connection. Relationship
traversal can allocate wrapper arrays even when a query stops testing early.
The [retained-heap measurements](benchmarking.md#heap-retained-across-captures)
compare these choices across repeated real captures.

# Query captured data

Capture once, then use standard collections. The [complete program](../examples/native_query.ml)
closes its blocking client before evaluating any of the functions below.
Follow the [README setup](../README.md#read-a-real-tmux-graph) first.

## Use a native predicate

<!-- example: examples/native_query.ml#native-filter -->

```ocaml
let active_ids snapshot =
  Snapshot.panes snapshot |> Iarray.to_seq |> Seq.filter Pane.active
  |> Seq.map Pane.id |> List.of_seq
```

`Snapshot.panes` returns an immutable array of captured panes. Converting it to
a sequence does not acquire anything. Repeated traversal sees captured values;
stateful callbacks supplied by an application can still behave differently.

## Describe a typed query

<!-- example: examples/native_query.ml#typed-filter -->

```ocaml
let roomy_terminals : Pane.t Expr.t =
  Expr.all
    [
      Expr.Bool.is_true Pane.Fields.active;
      Expr.Text.is_in Pane.Fields.current_command
        [ "cat"; "bash"; "zsh"; "nvim" ];
      Expr.Int.ge Pane.Fields.width 80;
    ]

let roomy_ids snapshot =
  Snapshot.panes snapshot |> Iarray.to_seq
  |> Query.matching roomy_terminals
  |> Seq.map Pane.id |> List.of_seq
```

`Expr.compile` returns an ordinary predicate. `Query.matching` compiles once
when constructed and preserves order and multiplicity. Field descriptors carry
both entity and value types, so invalid entity/operator combinations fail in
the compiler. Boolean `Expr.all []` is true and `Expr.any []` is false.

## Follow relationships without fetching

<!-- example: examples/native_query.ml#relationship-filter -->

```ocaml
let sessions_with_room snapshot =
  let expression =
    Expr.Rel.any Session.Relations.windows
      (Expr.Rel.any Window.Relations.panes roomy_terminals)
  in
  Snapshot.sessions snapshot |> Iarray.to_seq |> Query.matching expression
  |> Seq.map Session.name |> List.of_seq
```

Relationships traverse the complete captured graph. `Expr.Rel.any` over no
children is false; `all` and `none` over no children are true. Put conditions
inside one `any` when the same child must satisfy both. Two independent
existentials can match different children.

## Establish cardinality before acting

`Query.exactly_one` returns `No_match` or `Multiple_matches {at_least=2}` instead
of choosing the first element. It stops once it finds a second match; proving
uniqueness exhausts the remaining finite sequence. `one_or_none` returns an
option while retaining an ambiguity error. Duplicate entries count separately.

Select first, inspect the result, then submit a mutation. Selection does not
lock tmux; a target can disappear between observation and action. The
[control guide](control.md) explains that failure boundary.

## Decode portable query data explicitly

`Libtmux_json.Expr.of_string Model.pane` validates the shared scalar pane
subset of [`libtmux.filter/1`](query-interchange.md). It rejects duplicate/unknown
keys, wrong operand types, invalid UTF-8, oversized/deep documents and Java
regex. Native closures stay in `Seq.filter`; they have no portable wire identity.

`Libtmux.Plan.panes` compiles a source filter and retains the residual expression
without I/O. Inspect `source_filter` and use `Require_exact` to reject unsupported
lowering. Current client capture operations acquire the complete graph; they do
not execute these plans. The planner is a separate seam for acquisition adapters.
Conjunctions, disjunctions, negation and relationships require different lowering
rules; local sequence processing never issues a tmux query implicitly.

The [native reference](../lib/index.mld) executes a pure planning example with MDX.
The [architecture capability table](dev/adr/0001-native-ocaml-suite.md#compose-ordinary-predicates-with-typed-query-data)
distinguishes observation accessors, native expressions, JSON, planning and
client acquisition. An available accessor or format name need not be a
portable expression field.

[Field reference](fields.md) · [API](api.md) · [Guide](README.md)

# Share a scalar pane query

`Libtmux_json.Expr` reads and writes the following subset of
[`libtmux.filter/1`][java-wire]. Use `Model.pane` as the model witness. This
document defines the OCaml interoperability boundary; the
[query guide](queries.md) shows local evaluation and the
[complete JSON program](../examples/query_json.ml) demonstrates decoding,
encoding and structured errors.

## Document and nodes

A document has exactly `"schema"`, `"model"` and `"expr"` properties. The supported
values are `"libtmux.filter/1"` and `"pane"`. An expression is one of these nodes:

| `"node"` | Other required properties | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"compare"` | `"field"`, `"op"`, `"value"` | Compare one canonical scalar field |
| `"and"` | `"operands"`: expression array | Every operand matches; empty is true |
| `"or"` | `"operands"`: expression array | Any operand matches; empty is false |
| `"not"` | `"operand"`: expression | Negate one expression |

Property order is irrelevant. Duplicate, missing and unknown properties are
errors. Encoders preserve query meaning, not the original spelling: a
`"not_equals"` comparison can encode as `"not"` around `"equals"`.

## Fields and operators

Field names are case-sensitive canonical identities, not arbitrary accessors.

| Value type | Fields | Operators |
| --- | --- | --- |
| String | `"pane_id"`, `"pane_current_command"`, `"pane_title"`, `"pane_current_path"` | `"equals"`, `"not_equals"`, `"starts_with"`, `"ends_with"`, `"contains"`, `"in"` |
| Integer | `"pane_index"`, `"pane_width"`, `"pane_height"`, `"pane_left"`, `"pane_top"` | `"equals"`, `"not_equals"`, `"less_than"`, `"at_most"`, `"greater_than"`, `"at_least"` |
| Boolean | `"pane_active"` | `"equals"`, `"not_equals"` |

`"value"` has the field's JSON type. String `"in"` takes an array of strings and
matches equality with any member; an empty array matches nothing. Integers must
be integral JSON numbers in the signed 32-bit range, from −2,147,483,648 through
2,147,483,647. Floating-point values are rejected.

Text is valid UTF-8 with exact, case-sensitive matching. The codec performs no
normalization or case folding. Native OCaml predicates can process arbitrary
bytes, but invalid UTF-8 has no representation in this query schema.

Relationships, other models, native extension fields such as `"pane_dead"`,
optional fields such as `"pane_pid"`, integer membership and Java's `"matches"`
regex operator are outside this subset. Use native expressions or ordinary
`Seq.filter` for local behavior outside it.

## Bounds and errors

Both decoding and encoding enforce these limits:

| Resource | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| JSON document | 65,536 bytes |
| JSON nesting | 32 levels |
| Expression nodes | 1,024 |
| String membership values | 256 |

`Libtmux_json.Expr.of_string` checks input bytes and nesting before parsing.
`Libtmux_json.Expr.decode` validates
the supplied Yojson tree, including duplicate properties and the size of its
compact JSON representation. Encoding applies the same subset and bounds.

Failures return `Decode_error.t`: a JSON pointer, category and message. For
example, a string supplied to `"pane_width"` reports `Wrong_type` at
`/expr/value`. The decoder returns the first detected error, not an aggregate
validation report. It does not include the whole input in the error.

# Submit actions and retain their outcomes

Observations are local values. Client calls perform explicit I/O, and mutations
use targets bound to the source that produced them. Closing a client releases
its own transports. tmux then applies its configured lifetime: for example,
[the standalone programs](showcases.md) enable `exit-unattached` on their
private daemons so they exit after their final client detaches.

The [layout program](../examples/native_build.ml) creates a session, splits its
first pane and adds a logs window. It passes argv through `Spawn.Exec`, a working
directory and an environment value. `Spawn.Shell` explicitly requests shell
code. `send_text` is literal input; `send_keys [Key.Enter]` is a separate action.

A creation response returns the reported session, window and pane IDs without
an extra graph capture. Only the resource requested by that command is newly
created. A split's returned session and window are pre-existing containers.

## Choose a backend

Use `Libtmux_unix.Client` in a blocking script. Use `Libtmux_eio.Client` inside
an application-owned Eio switch, supplying the process manager and monotonic
clock. Clients are affine to their connecting domain. Immutable captured values
can be read from other domains; live client handles cannot move between them.

The Eio backend has client-owned workers for command draining and stream
reading. A cancelled waiter does not abandon a written request. Local scratch
filesystem work runs on a system thread. The blocking backend supports scoped
cancellation tokens signalled from another domain or systhread.

| Recovery concern | Eio | Blocking Unix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cancel one caller | Eio cancellation scope around `Client.await` | `Cancellation.with_` token passed to `Client.await` |
| Return after cancellation | The waiter raises while a client-owned fiber drains admitted work | The call drains before raising; one exchange timeout after detection bounds transport work |
| Inspect an outcome | `Operation.inspect`, on the connecting domain | `Operation.inspect`, on the connecting domain |
| Release resources | Close the client inside its application-owned switch | Close the client after the call returns |

The blocking bound covers transport draining. Local scratch I/O must still
finish before the call returns.

Captures, reads and subscriptions share the client's payload budget and process
slots. The [capacity guide](streaming.md#plan-shared-capacity) shows their combined
reservations and how to leave headroom for service operations.

Eio `Client.close` rejects new command and subscription admission as soon as
closing starts. Concurrent closes wait for the same teardown result. A later
close retains an earlier teardown failure; the closed state alone does not
prove resources were released. Inspect the client's `Cleanup` report for
secondary failures. Internal connection teardown also retains one completion,
so a concurrent failure path cannot skip cleanup already in progress.

The [complete recovery example](recovery.md) cancels an active waiter, awaits
the same retained operation and checks server state before its next mutation.

## Distinguish acknowledgement from completion

`submit` validates and reserves capacity without writing. Retain the operation
handle before awaiting it. `Operation.inspect` reads its state without I/O:
queued, not started, written, acknowledged, finished, or outcome unknown.

A reply can acknowledge a command while hooks or its completion marker remain
outstanding. Sending keys confirms tmux accepted input; it does not prove a
terminal program consumed it or completed work. A detach request does not prove
the peer exited. Use the relevant postcondition, rendered wait or external exit
signal for the task.

Expected failures use `result` and `Error.t`. Backend cancellation propagates
as cancellation. An uncertain result retains reported creation IDs and unresolved
owned buffers; it never becomes an instruction to retry the mutation.

When Eio's daemon watcher closes a connection, an in-flight operation retains
`Error.Disconnected` as its cause. An idle-reader failure retains its library
error. Explicit client closure uses `Error.Closed`. Inspect the retained receipt
to distinguish these reasons; each can leave an admitted mutation uncertain.

`Client.cleanup` retains process and descriptor cleanup diagnostics after
closure. Supply a `Cleanup.create ()` report through `~cleanup` before connecting
when diagnostics must survive failed setup or cancellation. The same option is
available on terminal attachment and workspace bootstrap. `Cleanup.inspect`
returns the cleanup phase, typed library error when available, original
exception and backtrace without I/O. The report retains at most 64 entries and
counts further issues; exception payloads can still retain substantial memory.
Reports and their diagnostics belong to the creating domain.

Cleanup attempts independent releases even when one fails. A primary exception
keeps its identity and backtrace; secondary failures go to the report. If there
is no primary failure, the first unrecovered cleanup failure is returned or
raised normally. A recovered fallback can still leave a diagnostic after a
successful return: failure to open a child pidfd skips TERM grace, forces
termination and reaps, while retaining the `Open_pidfd` issue.
Failed forced termination produces an `Unreaped_child` issue when exit cannot
be established without blocking. That issue does not prove resource release.
The [recovery example](recovery.md) keeps its report outside connection lifetime.

## Recover deliberately

A replacement daemon retires the connection generation. Reconnect explicitly,
capture again and establish cardinality before choosing a fresh target.
Old captured values remain readable, but their targets cannot silently move to
the new server.

Partial effects can remain after a later hook or command failure. Inspect the
retained receipt and current server state. Compensate only resources whose
creation is proven. A snapshot is an observation over an interval, and a
selection followed by mutation is not an atomic transaction.

Use the [recovery walkthrough](recovery.md) to follow this sequence through a
complete installed program, including cleanup of its own pane.

See [streaming](streaming.md) for Data/Gap/End and bounded queues, and
[compatibility](compatibility.md) for hook, PID-namespace and scratch-file
constraints. [Guide](README.md) · [API](api.md)

# Recover an operation after cancelling its waiter

For a creation followed by a failing tmux hook, see
[retained creation evidence](hook-recovery.md). That walkthrough inspects the
reported IDs after closing its client.

Retain the operation handle before awaiting it. Cancelling one Eio waiter leaves
admitted work under the client's ownership. Inspect that handle, await its
outcome and check the relevant server state before choosing another mutation.

This program uses a tmux `wait-for` barrier to keep an operation pending while
its waiter is cancelled. It then signals the barrier once and awaits the same
handle. A fresh capture checks the window's name before renaming it. The barrier
coordinates this example; it does not establish completion of a terminal
program. [Control](control.md) compares Eio and blocking cancellation timing.

## Run the complete program

Complete the [source installation](getting-started.md) and run from the cloned
repository. Start an empty private server:

```console
$ export LIBTMUX_RECOVERY_DIR="$(mktemp -d -t libtmux-ocaml-recovery.XXXXXX)"
```

```console
$ env -u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE tmux \
    -S "$LIBTMUX_RECOVERY_DIR/server" \
    -f /dev/null \
    new-session \
    -d \
    -s recovery-demo \
    -- "exec cat"
```

The fresh server's session ID is `$0`; quote it to preserve the literal ID:

```console
$ opam exec -- dune exec examples/native_recovery.exe -- \
    tmux "$LIBTMUX_RECOVERY_DIR/server" '$0'
```

Expected output is `waiter=cancelled; operation=retained`, followed by
`operation=finished; postcondition=recovery-complete` and
`cleanup-issues=0; omitted=0`. The program creates a window and removes its own pane afterward. It preserves the seed session and
other panes, and closes its client on success or failure.

Remove the private seed session and directory:

```console
$ env -u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE tmux \
    -S "$LIBTMUX_RECOVERY_DIR/server" \
    kill-session \
    -t '=recovery-demo'
```

```console
$ rm -f -- "$LIBTMUX_RECOVERY_DIR/server"
```

```console
$ rmdir "$LIBTMUX_RECOVERY_DIR"
```

## Inspect before acting

The [complete source](../examples/native_recovery.ml) uses installed public
libraries. Its Eio cancellation scope covers only the waiter. Client ownership
and cleanup remain outside that scope. A caller-owned `Cleanup` report is
created before connecting and inspected after closing. It remains accessible
if setup fails or cancellation prevents a client from being returned.

<!-- example: examples/native_recovery.ml -->

```ocaml
open Libtmux
module Client = Libtmux_eio.Client
module Operation = Libtmux_eio.Operation
module Cleanup = Libtmux_eio.Cleanup

let get = function
  | Ok value -> value
  | Error error -> failwith (Format.asprintf "%a" Error.pp error)

let protect ~finally use =
  match use () with
  | value ->
      finally ();
      value
  | exception error ->
      let backtrace = Printexc.get_raw_backtrace () in
      (try finally ()
       with cleanup ->
         Format.eprintf "cleanup failed: %s@." (Printexc.to_string cleanup));
      Printexc.raise_with_backtrace error backtrace

let cancel_waiter operation =
  let entered, enter = Eio.Promise.create () in
  let context = ref None in
  Eio.Fiber.pair
    (fun () ->
      try
        Eio.Cancel.sub (fun current ->
            context := Some current;
            Eio.Promise.resolve enter ();
            ignore (get (Client.await operation));
            failwith "wait completed before its release signal")
      with Eio.Cancel.Cancelled Exit -> ())
    (fun () ->
      Eio.Promise.await entered;
      Eio.Cancel.cancel (Option.get !context) Exit)
  |> ignore

let recover client session =
  let created =
    get
      (Client.create_window client session ~name:"recovery-pending"
         ~spawn:(Spawn.make (Exec { program = "/bin/cat"; args = [ "-u" ] })))
  in
  let channel =
    "libtmux-recovery-"
    ^ Generation.to_string (Source.generation (Client.source client))
  in
  let pending = ref None and release_attempted = ref false in
  let release () =
    if not !release_attempted then (
      release_attempted := true;
      get (Client.signal client channel))
  in
  protect
    ~finally:(fun () ->
      Eio.Cancel.protect (fun () ->
          protect
            ~finally:(fun () -> get (Client.kill_pane client created.pane))
            (fun () ->
              match !pending with
              | None -> ()
              | Some operation -> (
                  match get (Operation.inspect operation) with
                  | Operation.Queued -> get (Operation.cancel operation)
                  | Operation.Written | Operation.Acknowledged ->
                      release ();
                      get (Client.await operation)
                  | Operation.Not_started | Operation.Finished _
                  | Operation.Outcome_unknown _ ->
                      ()))))
    (fun () ->
      let operation =
        get (Client.submit client (Operations.wait_for channel))
      in
      pending := Some operation;
      ignore (get (Operation.await_stage operation `Acknowledged));
      cancel_waiter operation;
      (match get (Operation.inspect operation) with
      | Operation.Written | Operation.Acknowledged -> ()
      | Operation.Outcome_unknown receipt ->
          failwith
            (Format.asprintf "outcome unknown: %a" Error.pp receipt.cause)
      | _ -> failwith "expected a retained in-flight operation");
      print_endline "waiter=cancelled; operation=retained";
      release ();
      get (Client.await operation);
      (match get (Operation.inspect operation) with
      | Operation.Finished (Ok ()) -> ()
      | _ -> failwith "retained operation did not finish");
      let window =
        Snapshot.find_window
          (get (Client.capture client))
          (Window.Target.id created.window)
        |> Option.get
      in
      if Window.name window <> "recovery-pending" then
        failwith "postcondition changed; leave the next action to the caller";
      get
        (Client.rename_window client (Window.target window)
           ~name:"recovery-complete");
      let after =
        Snapshot.find_window (get (Client.capture client)) (Window.id window)
        |> Option.get
      in
      assert (Window.name after = "recovery-complete");
      Printf.printf "operation=finished; postcondition=%s\n" (Window.name after))

let () =
  if Array.length Sys.argv <> 4 then (
    prerr_endline "usage: native_recovery TMUX_BINARY SOCKET_PATH SESSION_ID";
    exit 2);
  Eio_main.run @@ fun env ->
  Eio.Switch.run @@ fun sw ->
  let cleanup = Cleanup.create () in
  protect
    ~finally:(fun () ->
      let report = get (Cleanup.inspect cleanup) in
      Iarray.iter
        (fun issue ->
          match issue.Cleanup.error with
          | Some error -> Format.eprintf "cleanup: %a@." Error.pp error
          | None ->
              Format.eprintf "cleanup: %s@."
                (Printexc.to_string issue.exception_))
        report.issues;
      Printf.printf "cleanup-issues=%d; omitted=%d\n"
        (Iarray.length report.issues)
        report.omitted)
    (fun () ->
      let client =
        get
          (Client.connect ~cleanup ~sw ~binary:Sys.argv.(1)
             ~process_mgr:(Eio.Stdenv.process_mgr env)
             ~mono_clock:(Eio.Stdenv.mono_clock env)
             (Endpoint.socket_path Sys.argv.(2)))
      in
      protect
        ~finally:(fun () ->
          Eio.Cancel.protect (fun () -> get (Client.close client)))
        (fun () ->
          let id = get (Session.Id.of_string Sys.argv.(3)) in
          let session =
            Snapshot.find_session (get (Client.capture client)) id |> Option.get
          in
          recover client (Session.target session)))
```

The release attempt is recorded before its I/O so cleanup cannot retry an
uncertain signal. The finally block cancels queued work, releases and drains a
live barrier, and removes only the pane whose creation was reported. Existing
panes remain outside that cleanup. A primary failure keeps its original
exception and backtrace; a later cleanup failure is reported separately. Both clients and operations stay on the
connecting domain.

## Interpret a retained state

[`Libtmux_eio.Operation.inspect`](../eio/libtmux_eio.mli) performs no I/O and
remains readable after client closure. A state describes this operation; it
does not prove a terminal program consumed input or exited.

| State | Next decision |
| --- | --- |
| `Queued` | Cancel before writing, or continue awaiting the same handle. |
| `Not_started` | The operation made no admitted effect; establish fresh preconditions before a new action. |
| `Written` or `Acknowledged` | Keep the handle. The client still owns completion; cancelling another waiter does not undo the write. |
| `Finished (Ok value)` | Use the result and check the task's relevant postcondition. |
| `Finished (Error error)` | Examine the error and current state; a later command or hook failure can follow an earlier effect. |
| `Outcome_unknown receipt` | Preserve the cause and reported creations. Reacquire observations explicitly and resolve uncertainty before another mutation. |

The example exercises active-waiter cancellation and retained completion. Its
unknown-outcome branch reports the cause and stops the next action. Transport
loss, a replacement daemon and uncertain mutation recovery require the retained
receipt and fresh observation; this program does not simulate those failures.
Closing a client does not terminate a borrowed tmux daemon.

For workspace automation, inspect the [execution receipt](workspaces.md#collisions-and-recovery)
and compensate only proven creations. For stream continuity loss, handle the
[Gap or End event](streaming.md) before choosing a fresh subscription.

# Observe output and wait for rendered text

Use [native_watch.ml](../examples/native_watch.ml) for a complete concurrent
literal-send, future-byte match and rendered-screen check. Its application owns
the Eio scheduler and switch. Use [native_wait.ml](../examples/native_wait.ml) to capture exactly one pane and
wait until its ordinary screen contains the supplied text. The example imports
the installed Eio client, owns its switch, uses an explicit socket, closes its
client and prints the matched pane ID. It requires an existing daemon and one
pane; absence and ambiguity remain errors.

`Client.wait_for_text` first subscribes, then captures the screen immediately.
Output invalidates that observation. Queued Data events are coalesced before
the next bounded capture; a queued Gap stops that coalescing. Membership and
overflow gaps cause fresh graph acquisition and subscription in the same
connection binding. A disconnected daemon or stream fails the wait.

Success returns a captured screen containing the text. Text that appears and
disappears between captures may be missed. Deadlines are checked between
acquisitions, whose in-flight I/O keeps the client's exchange timeout. A timed
out wait does not prove that text was absent in the past.

The wait releases its temporary subscription on every exit. An earlier error or
cancellation remains the primary result; `Client.cleanup` retains secondary
cleanup failures. If cleanup fails after a match or during gap recovery, the
wait fails instead of reporting success or opening another subscription.

Use `Client.subscribe` and `Subscription.next` for future output bytes. Data
retains every byte, including NUL and invalid UTF-8. Its cursor records a local
subscription generation and an observed byte offset. A cursor is neither a
snapshot timestamp nor a server-side history position. `poll` only removes a
queued event and performs no I/O.

`Subscription.wait_for_bytes` consumes those future events and matches across
event boundaries. Its nonempty pattern is limited to 64 KiB. It returns the
match's end cursor, possibly inside the last consumed Data event. A deadline
leaves the subscription active. A Gap returns `Output.Ended reason`; later
matching requires an explicit fresh capture and new subscription.

The defaults are 1 MiB and 1024 queued events per subscriber, at most 16 active
subscribers, and eight total client lanes including command/wait lanes. Reuse
one verified lane per covered session. Admission reserves bytes against the
shared 32 MiB budget. A full queue produces Gap then End rather than blocking
another subscriber or an independent command. Unknown loss has no byte count.
These limits apply together; [plan shared capacity](#plan-shared-capacity)
before combining many observers with captures and reads.

Coverage uses an observed session/window context and revalidates it during
admission. Layout or membership changes end continuity conservatively. Detaching
a stream leaves the primary client usable; a daemon replacement retires the
whole binding. New coverage always has a new subscription generation.

Eio readers belong to the client, use no application callbacks and keep running
when a subscriber stalls. The blocking backend advances all stream lanes during
`Subscription.next`. Cancellation closes the affected subscription and
propagates through the backend's cancellation mechanism. Client close releases
all owned lanes and retains terminal events; it leaves the daemon alive.

When a subscription releases the last user of a lane, close waits for its
owned helper to be reaped. Concurrent Eio subscription closes join that same
cleanup. Repeated closes preserve the first terminal reason and any cleanup
failure; unconsumed terminal events remain readable through `Subscription.poll`.

The [recovery program](recovery.md) shows how to cancel one operation waiter
while keeping its retained outcome available. Cancelling a subscription closes
that subscription; it does not cancel an already admitted command.

Neither interface establishes an atomic capture/stream barrier or reconstructs
terminal history. An immutable snapshot remains a separate captured value.

## Plan shared capacity

Every client has its own bounded payload budget and process-slot pool. The
blocking and Eio clients use the same accounting. An individually valid queue
or command can still return `Error.Capacity` when another reservation consumes
the available headroom:

| Resource | Current limit or reservation |
| --- | --- |
| Aggregate client payload | 32 MiB shared by queues, commands and operation scratch space |
| Admitted commands | 64; encoded payload accounting remains charged until completion or cancellation before writing |
| Admitted command bytes | 1 MiB shared across admitted operations; submission also temporarily reserves 2 MiB |
| Client process slots | 8, including the primary control client; each auxiliary slot reserves 128 KiB |
| Subscriptions | 16 active per client, sharing a verified stream lane per covered session |
| Subscriber queue | 1 MiB / 1024 events by default; reserve the full configured byte capacity even when empty |
| Graph or rendered capture | 16 MiB operation scratch reservation plus an 8 MiB control exchange |
| Option, environment or hook read | 16 MiB scratch reservation plus a temporary process slot |

The payload budget tracks library reservations. Caller-retained snapshots,
completed operation handles, receipts and exception payloads have their own
lifetimes, alongside runtime overhead, child-process memory and tmux's
allocations. See [observation retention](graph.md).

For example, sixteen default queues on one covered session reserve 16 MiB
plus that session's auxiliary slot. A subsequent capture or read cannot obtain
its scratch reservation. Even eight default queues leave insufficient room for
the capture's nested control exchange. Closing subscriptions releases their
reservations; the client remains usable after a capacity error.

| Empty queues, one covered session | Capture | Option read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 16 × 1 MiB | `Capacity` | `Capacity` |
| 8 × 1 MiB | `Capacity` | Fits the reservation budget |
| 7 × 1 MiB | Fits the reservation budget | Fits the reservation budget |
| 16 × 256 KiB | Fits the reservation budget | Fits the reservation budget |

These examples describe reservation accounting on a fixed one-pane graph.
Additional lanes, admitted commands and concurrent work consume more headroom.
A budget that fits still needs valid targets, available data and a responsive
daemon.

The [complete watcher](../examples/native_watch.ml) chooses its queue explicitly:

<!-- example: examples/native_watch.ml#bounded-subscription -->

```ocaml
let subscription =
  get
    (Client.subscribe ~capacity_bytes:(256 * 1024) ~capacity_events:256 client
       pane)
```

Its full program includes the client, pane acquisition, result handling, Eio
switch and cleanup. Choose a capacity for the burst your application can
consume; a smaller queue reaches `Gap Overflow` sooner when its reader stalls.

Slots need their own headroom. The primary client and seven distinct covered
sessions fill all eight slots, leaving none for a read process or `wait_for`.
If an application needs those operations, it can cap distinct covered sessions
at six while keeping one slot for service, accounting for any waits already
using slots. The library currently reserves no slot exclusively for service.
Several panes in the same session can share its stream lane.

Reducing queue capacities does not free process slots. Closing the last active
subscriber for a covered session releases its lane after owned-helper cleanup.
A separate client has its own budget and slots, but also its own source
generation: acquire observations on that client before using its targets.

## Recover after a gap

Close the ended subscription, capture the graph again, and establish fresh
coverage for the observed pane. This recovers future observation. Bytes lost
before the new subscription are still unavailable; a screen capture cannot
reconstruct their history.

The [complete recovery program](../examples/native_stream_recovery.ml) creates
a window running `cat`, observes a reply, then splits the window to trigger a
membership gap. It handles that gap, removes the extra pane and closes the old
subscription. It captures the original pane again, subscribes, and observes
new input with a different cursor generation:

<!-- example: examples/native_stream_recovery.ml#recover-coverage -->

```ocaml
let recover_coverage client id (previous : Output.cursor) =
  let fresh = capture_pane client id in
  let after =
    with_subscription client fresh (fun subscription ->
        echo client fresh subscription "after-gap")
  in
  if Generation.equal previous.generation after.generation then
    failwith "new subscription reused the old cursor generation";
  print_endline "coverage=fresh; cursor-generation=new; future=after-gap"
```

The source contains the imports, scheduler, cleanup and matching helpers.
`capture_pane` fails if the pane disappeared. `with_subscription` admits coverage
before `echo` sends input and awaits its reply concurrently. The
example never reconnects, reuses an old cursor or retries an uncertain mutation.
It removes only panes whose creation returned successfully, leaving any foreign
panes untouched. Primary exceptions survive secondary cleanup failures.

Creation here uses convenience calls. Cancellation before one returns can leave
a creation whose ID the caller never received. For creation outcomes that must
survive waiter cancellation, retain `Client.submit`'s handle before `Client.await`,
as shown in [operation recovery](recovery.md). An uncertain outcome does not
authorize a retry or deletion of an unproven resource.

```console

    -S "$LIBTMUX_STREAM_RECOVERY_DIR/server" \
    -f /dev/null \
    new-session \
    -d \
```

Expected output is `gap=membership-changed; history=unavailable`, followed by

This repository is one Dune project with separately installable opam packages.

Owned-child cleanup sends TERM, allows a 200 ms cooperative grace, then sends
KILL if necessary and reaps the child. The policy covers control, read-process
and terminal helpers; it never sends these signals to the daemon. Eio waits
allow other fibers to progress. The grace applies per helper, not to the whole
client, and cannot bound uninterruptible kernel work or scratch-file completion.
Caller-owned `Cleanup` reports retain secondary process and descriptor failures
without replacing native cancellation or the primary exception. Independent
releases are still attempted. A failed KILL only permits a nonblocking exit
check; an unconfirmed exit is reported as `Unreaped_child`. Concurrent Eio
client closes await one retained teardown result. The Eio runtime owns its pipe
ends explicitly and joins their readiness waiters before closing them. Process
I/O rechecks closure after yielding, preventing access to reused descriptors.
A private Eio process owner keeps its reaper alive through cancellation and
switch release; callers join its completed teardown. Shutdown regressions cover
both Eio's Linux and POSIX backends on Linux. This does not add platform support.
New commands and subscriptions are rejected as soon as client close starts.
Connection and subscription teardown also retain one completion: overlapping
Eio callers join it, and later calls preserve its failure.

The shutdown regression checks stopped helpers and helpers that survive TERM
and input closure, while keeping the parent and its Eio switch alive to verify
reaping. These are injected helper failures, not naturally reproduced hangs in
a supported tmux daemon. Blocking readiness uses `poll`; ready reads, ready
writes and deadlines work above descriptor 1100. Terminal attachment and
cancellation also have high-descriptor evidence on the previously tested
3.3/3.3a/3.4/3.8 fixtures. See the
[architecture's cleanup boundary](dev/adr/0001-native-ocaml-suite.md#share-protocol-semantics-while-preserving-each-runtimes-cancellation).

The near-limit [mixed workload](benchmarking.md#mixed-commands-stream-pressure-and-membership-changes)
reproduces a tmux 3.4 daemon crash in the control-client detach notification
path. The exact 3.8 source includes the upstream null-state guard. An earlier
3.3 observer-command failure remains unattributed. Passing ordinary client
checks does not close either mixed-workload failure.

The I/O packages require Linux pidfds, the same PID namespace as the daemon,
and shared local scratch storage. A socket pathname does not prove those
conditions. Each connection has its own generation; a replacement daemon never
inherits old targets. Closing a client releases its own processes and leaves
the daemon running.

The blocking client accepts a scoped `Cancellation` token that another domain
or systhread can cancel. It drains admitted work before raising
`Cancellation.Cancelled`. The drain has at most one exchange timeout from
detection; subsequent owned-child cleanup has its separate cooperative grace.
The operation handle retains success, failure or uncertainty. Eio cancellation
releases the waiter immediately while a client-owned fiber drains the work.
Local scratch I/O must finish in either case; Eio performs it on a system
thread. Filesystem failures have a distinct error from transport disconnects.

Pane PIDs and client terminal heights can be absent. The model exposes these as
options; a control client without a started terminal has no reported height.
tmux itself sanitizes names on older releases and rejects some names on newer
releases. Captures preserve the observed value rather than reconstructing the
argument originally submitted by another client.

Control commands use ASCII escapes for non-ASCII bytes because tmux 3.3's
command-string lexer can confuse a signed `0xff` byte with EOF. Metadata uses
tmux's `q` format modifier and preserves physical newlines. A fixed read probe
detects the additional visual escaping used by tmux 3.4 before decoding it.
Control clients must request UTF-8 mode so locale-dependent sanitization cannot
alter captured bytes.

An end guard acknowledges a command. Completion requires the operation's
postcondition or a following marker on its lane. A control client may exit
with status 1 after an earlier command failed, even when later commands and
shutdown succeeded. Tests retain that distinction.

The optional JSON codec supports the scalar pane registry and Boolean nodes
from Java's [`libtmux.filter/1`](query-interchange.md) at revision
`e8a39689d8d60968ac978a1dd2a89c6112333896`. Both implementations agree on 66
captured-value cases and read each other's encoded queries. Numeric operands
use signed 32-bit bounds. Regex, relationship documents, numeric membership
and native extension fields remain unsupported in this wire schema.
The [conformance procedure](../test/conformance/README.md) rebuilds the peers
from identified inputs and retains both codec directions and artifact digests.
It is a separate qualification command, not part of ordinary hosted OCaml CI.

Reproduce native checks with the commands in
[CONTRIBUTING.md](../.github/CONTRIBUTING.md). The fixture builders use official
release archives and retain archive and binary digests under `scratch/tmux/`.

Environment reads use a bounded read-only process on the same daemon. The
client checks its reported PID and the original pidfd after collecting the
complete response. Values may contain control-marker text without entering
the control parser. Replacement, malformed data, truncated output and capacity
failures never become a successful empty table. This route does not execute
mutations or reconnect the primary lane.

Scoped options preserve scalar types, sparse array indexes and local versus
inherited entries. Bulk inherited enumeration follows tmux and includes only
built-ins; `read_option` resolves a named inherited user option. Descriptors are
recorded for every supported release in the [option catalog](options.md). tmux
fills the lowest unused indexes when appending array elements.

Hook commands keep names and arguments separate. Built-in hook arrays report
synchronous failures; earlier effects remain after a later command fails. Named
`@` hooks can be configured, read and removed, but `run_hook` rejects them because
tmux may hide parse failures in the server log. Hooks that print arbitrary output
remain outside the supported control transport contract.

Captured client names belong to a connection generation but may be reused within
it. Operations address the client currently bearing that name. A detach request
confirms command processing, not peer exit; callers need separate exit evidence.
Switching an existing client does not create a new terminal.

`Terminal.attach_current` opens an interactive terminal against an explicit
endpoint and session ID. This separate utility is unbound: an ID can refer to a
different daemon if the endpoint changes. It accepts no captured target and
never retries or starts a daemon. Both backends wait for the terminal client to
exit and reap it on cancellation. Supplied terminal streams remain caller-owned.

The generated [format catalog](formats.md) records exact-release availability
and callback contexts. Local `Formats.lookup` distinguishes captured values,
missing values, unacquired fields and fields unsupported by that release.
It does not perform arbitrary format acquisition. Generated
[operation conveniences](operations.md) share the same command constructors
between Unix and Eio; the installed-consumer test exercises both adapters.

# Testing and CI

Use Alcotest for typed values and lifecycle invariants, `ppx_expect` for readable
output contracts, and QCheck for generated semantic cases. All three run through
Dune. The pure runtime library uses the standard library; the PPX is a test-only
dependency.

The [cardinality tests](../test/core_test.ml) compare typed results using an
[`Alcotest.testable`](https://mirage.github.io/alcotest/alcotest/Alcotest/index.html#type-testable)
with `Cardinality.pp_error`. A failure displays the expected
and actual values, including the error variant's meaning. Comparing a Boolean
expression would only report `true` versus `false`. Keep testable printers small
and show the values needed to understand the failure.

The [expect tests](../test/diagnostics_expect.ml) place expected diagnostic text
beside the code that prints it. A mismatch produces a diff and a `.corrected`
file. Inspect the changed meaning before promoting an expectation. Stable query
explanations, error messages and CLI output fit this style. Avoid snapshotting
timestamps, random IDs or whole server captures to test a small invariant.

[QCheck cases](../test/query_test.ml) compare typed-expression evaluation against
native predicates with generated inputs. A fixed seed makes the current suite
reproducible; shrinking helps explain counterexamples. Properties supplement the
small authored edge cases and live tmux checks.

Run the unit, expect, property and compile-failure suite:

```console
$ opam exec -- dune runtest --force
```

Cold PPX driver compilation belongs to setup or an outer build. Time the warm
test command separately and retain the existing inner/mid budgets. Native and
installed-consumer checks belong to the outer loop because they launch processes
and own real tmux servers.

Run the implemented native contract suite against one explicit release binary:

```console
$ opam exec -- python3 test/native_suite.py /path/to/tmux
```

The [CI workflow](../.github/workflows/ocaml.yml) uses exactly OCaml 5.5.2,
Alcotest 1.9.1, `ppx_expect` v0.17.3 and QCheck 0.91. It checks authored manifests,
builds/odoc, generated files, formatting, unit/expect/property cases, and two
native release cells: tmux 3.3a (oldest supported) and 3.8 (newest stable).
Every intermediate release remains supported. Pure assertions check version
boundaries and catalog availability throughout the range. Each native cell
installs the packages into a temporary prefix and runs a consumer outside the
checkout. Consumer features still in development need their own later
acceptance gates.

The [Java/OCaml conformance procedure](../test/conformance/README.md) prepares a
pinned Java peer separately, verifies artifact hashes and runs both evaluators
and codec directions. Its fixtures and failure diagnostics are retained per
run. This qualification is outside ordinary OCaml CI and the fast test loops.

The CLI document check exercises regular files and piped input on both Eio
backends, including the inclusive 64 KiB boundary. Pass `--directory` to
exercise a mounted filesystem using an owned temporary directory:

```console
$ opam exec -- python3 test/workspace_document_test.py
```

`ocaml/setup-ocaml` caches opam and the switch. The tmux composite action caches
only an installed prefix, keyed by source, runner image/version, architecture,
compiler, package versions and build/probe recipes. Dependencies are installed
before validating either hits or misses. A restored binary must match its hash,
report the exact release and pass an owned-daemon probe with verified teardown.
Rejected caches rebuild; no broad restore key reuses a binary from another
environment. Save a validated installation before running library tests.

The cache design adapts the [Go port's pinned implementation](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-go/blob/d8ea6f77ede9f75e96af78719c8c1707fc47bdfb/.github/scripts/tmux_build.py).
The APIs and testing styles follow the primary documentation for
[setup-ocaml](https://github.com/ocaml/setup-ocaml/tree/ff66428f72b64472e749b22e0ad4dded4b2ddca6),
[Alcotest](https://github.com/mirage/alcotest/tree/1.9.1),
[ppx_expect](https://github.com/janestreet/ppx_expect/tree/v0.17.3), and
[Dune tests](https://dune.readthedocs.io/en/stable/tests.html).

# Measure capture, concurrency and output delivery

The [capture benchmark](../bench/capture.py) compares serial blocking and Eio
capture on one owned graph: one session, four windows and sixteen panes. Each
sample captures the graph 100 times by default and selects active panes using both a
compiled expression and a native predicate over each same snapshot.

The harness checks exact ordered IDs across captures and modes, one observed
tmux client and one child process per mode, and zero attached clients afterward.
Owned fixture teardown verifies pane and daemon exit. Both modes reuse one
bound connection for their captures; they perform no per-object acquisition.

## Reproduce

Prepare the [exact release fixture](../.github/CONTRIBUTING.md#owned-tmux-fixtures),
then build the benchmark outside normal test loops:

```console
$ opam exec -- dune build bench/capture.exe
```

Run it with Python 3.11 or newer. Choose a new output file each time:

```console
$ opam exec -- python3 bench/capture.py scratch/tmux/tmux-3.8/tmux \
    --iterations 100 \
    --repeat 5 \
    --output scratch/capture-baseline.json
```

the capture loop and client closure. Fixture creation and compilation are

waits and checks subscription cleanup. One primary client becomes two while a
stream lane is active; both observed client and child-process counts are
checked. No clients remain after closure, and owned pane/daemon exit is verified.

Each option read starts a read-only tmux process inside the client's pump.

## Mixed commands, stream pressure and membership changes

The [mixed-load benchmark](../bench/mixed.py) overlaps retained command
submissions, seven fast stream readers, seven deliberately stalled readers,
membership changes and cancellation. Its default runs three waves with eight
command workers and four attributed output frames per stream lane. It adds no
work to the unit-test loops.

Build the executable separately:

```console
$ opam exec -- dune build bench/mixed.exe
```

Run the bounded workload against one owned release fixture:

```console
$ opam exec -- python3 bench/mixed.py scratch/tmux/tmux-3.8/tmux \
    --output scratch/mixed-baseline.json
```

Each wave submits 64 commands without yielding and requires the 65th to reject
with the declared admission limit. Eight queued operations are cancelled before
writing; their handles retain `Not_started`. Sixteen subscribers occupy seven
shared session lanes. Together with the load connection's primary lane this
reaches its eight-lane limit; a separate controller connection sends output and
changes membership. The seventeenth subscriber and an additional session lane
must reject with their specific capacity errors. These expected rejections are
recorded separately from correctness failures.

Commands set unique user-option names and values. The receipt retains operation
IDs, worker IDs, submission indexes and the actual order in which awaiters
observe results. It verifies every resulting option value, including absence
for cancelled operations. Ordinary mutations use the retained control lane;
`read_option` verification runs afterward through its temporary subprocess route
and has a separate phase duration. Each verified option emits its operation ID,
completed count and read duration before the observer handshake. The validation
phase includes those handshakes; individual read durations exclude them.
The observer acknowledgements and resource queries add measured overhead, so
these are instrumented workload timings.

Fast streams must deliver exact ordered bytes with continuous generation and
byte offsets. Tiny unconsumed queues must report `Gap Overflow`, then `End`.
Splitting and removing a temporary pane changes a watched window's membership;
affected readers must report `Gap Membership_changed`, then `End`. Explicit
readmission uses a fresh observation and generation. Unchanged lanes continue independently; the receipt requires observed stream
progress while commands remain pending in each wave. Each wave also cancels an active observer after
its retained wait reaches `Acknowledged`, releases the wait through the
controller, and checks the eventual result before and after client closure.

Native event callbacks synchronously sample owned Linux process trees before
yielding to telemetry, retaining their occurrence-time pending-command counts.
Progress handshakes separately sample process trees and attached tmux clients,
including while the churn pane is alive. Emission timestamps and counts stay
separate from event occurrence; queued telemetry cannot manufacture overlap. Raw records distinguish
the Python harness, OCaml process, daemon, command-client children and pane
children. RSS/FD/process/client maxima are maxima of these observations;
per-process RSS high-water marks come from the kernel. They do not establish
continuous aggregate resource peaks. The controller contributes a primary client
and, during its retained wait, an auxiliary client in addition to the load
connection's eight clients. The sampler's own retained pidfds affect its FD count.

Per-worker receipts report completed quotas, cancellation counts, latency samples
and first/last observation times. They characterize this bounded workload rather
than proving scheduler fairness, a service-level objective or general capacity.
The 1 MiB queued-byte and 32 MiB payload limits are recorded source constraints;
this workload pressures admission counts, subscriber counts and lane counts,
not those byte maxima. No automatic retries or timeout increases hide a failure.

Exercise teardown after interruption with a new output file:

```console
$ opam exec -- python3 bench/mixed.py scratch/tmux/tmux-3.8/tmux \
    --rounds 1 \
    --frames 2 \
    --inject-failure \
    --output scratch/mixed-interrupted.json
```

`EXPECTED_FAILURE` means the harness intentionally interrupted the native
process while a temporary pane was alive. It still requires owned daemon,
pane and command-client exit, reaping, zero remaining children and removal of
the private fixture directory. Unexpected errors or failed cleanup produce
`FAIL`; an interruption is not a successful workload measurement.

The [summary](../bench/results/mixed-20261108.json) records each outcome and
source identity. The linked gzip archives contain the complete JSON receipts;
the summary includes their compressed and uncompressed SHA-256 digests.

Raw results retain exact source and executable hashes, fixture-helper hash,
versions, command arguments, workload bounds, host load, resource observations
and cleanup receipts. Keep failed receipts beside passing measurements when
assessing a release. Current collector qualification is **PARTIAL** across the supported releases:

# Current capabilities and adoption gaps

The immutable model, typed queries, native Linux clients and output observation
have real-tmux evidence at the active tmux endpoints, 3.3a and 3.8. Intermediate
releases remain supported throughout 3.3a–3.8. The installed
workspace CLI also passes those cells. The final suite review remains unfinished.
No package or hosted-documentation release has been published.

## What an application can use

Capture a complete graph, retain it after closing the client, traverse shared
windows through session-specific links, filter with native predicates or typed
expressions, and establish cardinality before an explicit mutation. Native
operations cover sessions, windows, panes, captured clients, layouts,
environment, options and hooks. Both blocking and Eio transports retain
operation outcomes and expose bounded subscriptions.

The [compatibility table](compatibility.md) identifies qualified components.
The [examples](README.md) are installed, compiled and executed against owned
servers; they cover graph links, query results, created resources, literal
input, streaming, rendered waits and client teardown.

[Recorded benchmarks](benchmarking.md) cover blocking/Eio capture, graphs up to
256 panes, concurrent requests, OCaml heap allocation, client/daemon CPU,
future-output latency and cancellation cleanup. Their raw data preserves the
workload, source identities and host conditions.

The workspace model, JSON loader, blocking/Eio executors and installed CLI are
implemented. The [workspace guide](workspaces.md) executes the installed command
through validation, planning, apply, receipt inspection and owned cleanup.
Live tests cover partial effects, compensation, append isolation, stale plans,
cancellation journals and bootstrap on fresh and existing daemons. Cleanup
targets only proven newly created panes; foreign panes moved into a new window
remain. Versioned advisory plans and execution receipts preserve errors,
creation IDs and cleanup outcomes; output documents cannot be replayed as
operational input. CLI checks also cover malformed input, collisions, missing
endpoints, interrupted apply, changed documents and stalled or broken stdout.

## Engineering assessment

For a Linux application needing immutable tmux observations and explicit native
control, the model and clients are candidates for adoption with the documented
constraints. Suite adoption still needs the documentation and qualification
above. Maintainer count and alpha status do not decide that
assessment; observable behavior and recovery do.

An adopting engineer should expect explicit endpoint selection, client lifetime,
command uncertainty and stream gaps. The package should keep these visible.
Implicit reconnects, callback-driven property acquisition, a mandatory query
wrapper or a required runtime for pure filtering would make the API harder to
reason about.

A 9.5/10 whole-package rating is not established. Hosted documentation and
final qualification have open gates. Documentation
quality cannot substitute for those results. [Testing](testing.md) describes
current evidence and how examples are kept in sync with source.

MCP integration is excluded by project policy. Its SDK, conformance and host
integration are outside the adoption criteria. The supported automation
surfaces are native OCaml APIs and the workspace CLI; see
[package boundaries](packages.md).

# Create a workspace from JSON

`tmux-workspace` validates a JSON configuration, previews an advisory plan, and
applies a fresh plan to an explicit socket. Install it through the
[source installation](../README.md#install-from-source); `opam install .`
includes the CLI. Run this guide from the repository root.

`check` performs no tmux I/O. `plan` observes the endpoint and never starts a
daemon. `apply` rereads the document, checks current state, then executes ordered
actions. A preview is not a transaction or an executable target.

## Define the layout

The shipped [project.json](../examples/workspace/project.json) creates an
`editor` window with two panes and a `logs` window with one. Each pane runs
`/bin/cat -u` directly, keeping the demonstration alive without a shell command.

<!-- example: examples/workspace/project.json -->

```json
{
  "schema": "libtmux.workspace/1",
  "session": "ocaml-project",
  "cwd": ".",
  "width": 120,
  "height": 40,
  "environment": {"PROJECT": "ocaml"},
  "options": [{"name": "@project", "kind": "text", "value": "ocaml"}],
  "windows": [
    {
      "name": "editor",
      "layout": "even-horizontal",
      "panes": [
        {"exec": ["/bin/cat", "-u"]},
        {"exec": ["/bin/cat", "-u"], "direction": "right"}
      ]
    },
    {"name": "logs", "panes": [{"exec": ["/bin/cat", "-u"]}]}
  ]
}
```

Relative directories resolve against the JSON file's directory. Environment
values merge from session to window to pane. `exec` supplies literal argv;
`shell` explicitly requests shell interpretation. They are mutually exclusive.
Omitting both uses tmux's default command. `startup` entries send literal text
followed by Enter; they do not wait for a command to finish.

## Validate, preview and apply

This walkthrough uses a private server and an empty tmux configuration. The
`seed` session keeps the server alive while the CLI creates the project.
Inherited `TMUX` and `TMUX_PANE` do not select the endpoint.

<!-- workspace-walkthrough:begin -->

```console
$ export LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR="$(mktemp -d -t libtmux-ocaml-workspace.XXXXXX)"
```

Copying the file also makes its working directory the private directory:

```console
$ cp examples/workspace/project.json "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/project.json"
```

```console
$ opam exec -- tmux-workspace check "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/project.json"
```

Expected output: `Valid workspace "ocaml-project": 2 windows, 3 panes`.

```console
$ env -u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE tmux \
    -S "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/server" \
    -f /dev/null \
    new-session \
    -d \
    -s seed \
    -- "exec cat"
```

```console
$ opam exec -- tmux-workspace plan \
    --socket "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/server" \
    --require-existing \
    "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/project.json"
```

The plan lists session creation, settings, the split and layout, and the logs
window. Applying it requires the original configuration:

```console
$ opam exec -- tmux-workspace apply \
    --socket "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/server" \
    --require-existing \
    --json \
    "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/project.json" \
    > "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/receipt.json"
```

The receipt uses [`libtmux.workspace-receipt/1`](../json/libtmux_json.mli).
On success, `status` is
`succeeded`; `failed`, `uncertain` and `skipped` are empty. Each creation records
the IDs returned by tmux. Check the resulting windows independently:

```console
$ env -u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE tmux \
    -S "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/server" \
    list-windows \
    -t '=ocaml-project' \
    -F '#{window_name}:#{window_panes}'
```

Expected output is `editor:2` followed by `logs:1`.

Remove only the sessions this walkthrough created:

```console
$ env -u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE tmux \
    -S "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/server" \
    kill-session \
    -t '=ocaml-project'
```

```console
$ env -u TMUX -u TMUX_PANE tmux \
    -S "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/server" \
    kill-session \
    -t '=seed'
```

```console
$ rm -f -- "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/server" \
    "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/project.json" \
    "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR/receipt.json"
```

```console
$ rmdir "$LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_DIR"
```

<!-- workspace-walkthrough:end -->

Without `--require-existing`, `apply` can start a missing endpoint by creating
the requested session. That server uses the normal tmux configuration. Closing
the CLI's client leaves the server running; its appearance does not grant
daemon ownership. `plan` on a missing endpoint checks the local tmux version
and returns a bootstrap plan without creating the socket.

## Collisions and recovery

An existing session name fails with exit 4 by default. `--append` adds new
windows to that session and rejects window-name collisions. Append never
changes the existing session's options or environment; omit those session
settings from an append document. It preserves existing panes.

Use `--json` on `check` or `plan` to obtain `document_digest`, then pass that
value through `--expect-document` on apply. A changed document fails before
endpoint I/O. The digest does not lock tmux state. Each apply builds and
rechecks its own plan on the current connection generation.

On failure or SIGINT, inspect the receipt before deciding what to do next.
Default compensation kills only panes whose creation the journal proved, in
reverse order. A foreign pane moved into a new window remains. `--keep-partial`
retains proven creations instead. Cleanup failures and creations whose IDs
could not be bound remain explicit. Never rerun an uncertain mutation solely
because its caller was interrupted.

The [retained-operation example](recovery.md) demonstrates waiter recovery.
The [native workspace example](workspace-recovery.md) interrupts an apply,
inspects its journal after client cleanup and verifies compensation. Read the
available journal, identify proven effects, then choose another explicit action.
A saved JSON receipt describes observations; it is not an executable target or
a transaction to replay.

The execution journal is retained in process memory. `await` initiates steps
only once for a particular execution handle; a new handle or CLI invocation
starts a new execution. Operation IDs correlate receipts and do not suppress
duplicates. Neither a retained handle nor an exported receipt is a durable
write-ahead log. Compensation cannot undo files, network requests or other
effects of the programs launched in panes.

| Exit | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Validation, planning or apply succeeded |
| 2 | Invalid arguments or document |
| 3 | Required endpoint missing |
| 4 | Collision, changed document or stale plan |
| 5 | Failed, partial or uncertain apply; inspect the receipt |
| 6 | Transport, capability or result-delivery failure |
| 130 | SIGINT; the available journal is emitted within the cleanup bound |

SIGINT does not undo admitted commands. Receipt output is bounded; a blocked or
broken stdout cannot produce a successful exit. Forced process termination
cannot promise a delivered receipt. Expected failures are distinct from Eio
cancellation in the native API, which propagates cancellation to the caller.

## Bounds and native callers

Documents use UTF-8 JSON with a 64 KiB input bound and depth limit 32. Unknown
and duplicate properties fail. Configurations allow at most 64 windows and 256
panes; a plan allows at most 4096 actions. Plans and receipts have a 4 MiB output
bound. Plans omit environment values, option values and startup text. They can
still contain command arguments and paths; treat them as application data.

For native code, use `Libtmux_json.Workspace.of_string`,
`Libtmux_workspace.Plan.make`, and the backend's `Workspace.submit` or
`Workspace.submit_bootstrap`. `inspect` reads the retained journal locally;
`await` performs I/O. The application owns the Eio switch and scheduler.
The [native bootstrap walkthrough](bootstrap.md) starts one private session
without a JSON dependency and captures its graph through the resulting client.
See the [API reference](api.md), [control outcomes](control.md) and
[compatibility evidence](compatibility.md).

# Interrupt a workspace and inspect its journal

Eio cancellation interrupts the remaining workspace steps. The client still
owns written commands, and the workspace attempts protected compensation for
reported creations. Keep the execution handle outside the cancellation and
client lifetimes, then read `Libtmux_eio.Workspace.inspect` after cleanup.

This program plans two windows, interrupts the first creation at a tmux hook,
and checks that the reported session ID is absent after compensation. Its final
journal remains readable after the Eio switch closes both clients.
See [compatibility](compatibility.md) for current qualification limits.

```console
$ export LIBTMUX_WORKSPACE_RECOVERY_DIR="$(mktemp -d -t libtmux-ocaml-workspace-recovery.XXXXXX)"
```

```console
    new-session \
    -d \
```

```console
    -g \
    after-new-session \
```
